items.prompt: What does Git actually store when you make a commit?
choices: A diff (line-by-line changes) from the previous commit
A full snapshot of the entire project, with unchanged files deduplicated by content
A copy of only the files you explicitly listed in the commit message
A compressed archive of the working directory, re-copied in full every time
items.explanation: Git conceptually stores a full snapshot per commit, not a diff — diffs are computed on demand for display. Snapshots stay cheap because unchanged file content is deduplicated by its content hash, not re-copied, so committing cost is proportional to what changed, not total project size.
items.reference:
📸 Every commit = a full snapshot, not a diff
🔗 Unchanged files: referenced, not re-copied
🐌 Diffs are computed later, only for display

Why: content-addressing means an unchanged file is stored once and pointed to by every commit that includes it, so "full snapshot" doesn't mean "full re-copy."
items.learnMore:
Snapshot, not diff

A word processor's "track changes" stores edits relative to a base document — reconstructing any past version means replaying every edit in order. Git stores each commit as a complete, independently addressable state of the whole project. git diff and git log -p compute a diff between two snapshots on the fly, purely for human reading — nothing about that computed diff is what's actually persisted to disk. This is also why checking out any past commit is a direct lookup, not a replay of history from the start.

items.prompt: A teammate says "Git must store a growing list of line-by-line edits, like a word processor's track changes, because that's the only way `git log -p` can show you a diff." What's wrong with that reasoning?
choices: Nothing is wrong — that's exactly how Git works internally
`git log -p` computes the diff by comparing two stored snapshots at display time; the diff itself is never what's stored
Git only shows diffs for text files, so the reasoning is half right
Git stores diffs, but only for the most recent 50 commits, to save space
items.explanation: The diff shown by `git log -p` is derived, not stored — Git compares the two full snapshots (the commit and its parent) at the moment you ask, and computes what's different. What's actually persisted on disk is the pair of complete snapshots, not a pre-recorded diff between them.

🔗 Unchanged files: referenced, not re-copied
🐌 Diffs are computed later, only for display

Why: content-addressing means an unchanged file is stored once and pointed to by every commit that includes it, so "full snapshot" doesn't mean "full re-copy."

items.prompt: If commits are full snapshots, why doesn't every commit take as long, and as much disk space, as copying the entire project?
choices: Because Git secretly deletes old commits after a while
Because unchanged files are deduplicated by content and referenced, not physically re-copied, so cost tracks what changed
Because Git only stores snapshots for the 10 most recent commits
It does — every commit costs the same as a full project copy, which is why repositories grow so large
items.explanation: "Full snapshot" describes the logical content each commit represents, not a claim that every file gets physically re-copied. Content-addressed storage means an unchanged file's bytes already exist in the object store from a previous commit, so the new commit just points to them again.

items.prompt: You edit a file, then run `git add file.txt`, but haven't run `git commit` yet. Which statement is true?
choices: The change is already permanently in the project's history
The change is staged (marked for the next snapshot) but not yet committed to history
Nothing has happened yet — `git add` only previews the change
The change is committed, but not yet pushed to a remote
items.explanation: The three-state model (working directory → staging area → repository) means staging is a real, distinct middle state: `git add` moves a change into 'will be part of the next snapshot,' but only `git commit` actually writes that snapshot into permanent history.
items.reference:
💻 Working directory — files on disk right now
📥 Staging area — marked for the next snapshot
🗄️ Repository — permanent, committed history

Why: git add and git commit are two separate steps precisely because staging and history are two separate states.
items.learnMore:
The three-state model

Manual-copy workflows have no equivalent of staging — every save is all-or-nothing, the entire current state of the folder. Git's staging area lets you build a commit out of only some of your current changes: edit five files, but only three of them belong together conceptually, and you can stage and commit just those three, then handle the other two separately. This is what keeps commit history readable as a series of coherent, describable changes instead of one giant "various fixes" commit.

items.prompt: You've staged `config.json` with `git add`, then immediately edit `config.json` again without re-staging. What does `git status` show?
choices: Nothing — the second edit automatically updates the staged version
Both a staged change and a separate unstaged change for the same file
An error — you can't edit a file after staging it
The staged version is discarded, and only the newest edit is tracked
items.explanation: Staging captures the file's content at the moment `git add` ran — it's a snapshot of that instant, not a live link to the file. Editing the file again afterward creates a second, separate difference between the working directory and the staged version, and `git status` reports both.
items.reference:
💻 Working directory — files on disk right now
📥 Staging area — marked for the next snapshot
🗄️ Repository — permanent, committed history

Why: git add and git commit are two separate steps precisely because staging and history are two separate states.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario, Priya's login fix vanished from Alex's copy with no explanation. Which underlying problem with manual copies actually caused that?
choices: Zip files are inherently unreliable and corrupt data randomly
Neither copy recorded a relationship to the other, so there was no way to detect or combine the two people's independent changes
Alex used the wrong compression format
Email attachments strip file changes automatically
items.explanation: A zip file is a dead end — it has no recorded link to whatever it was copied from, and no mechanism for combining two independently-edited copies. The failure wasn't a technical glitch in zipping; it was the total absence of a relationship between the two saves that could have been detected and merged.
items.reference:
📁 Two zips, no recorded relationship between them
❓ No way to detect they diverged from the same starting point
🚫 No mechanism to combine both people's changes

Why: a commit's parent pointer is exactly the missing link — it's what lets Git detect two branches diverged from a common point and merge them.
items.learnMore:
Why manual copies fail at scale

Manual copies fail for three compounding reasons: no record of why something changed (a filename isn't a commit message), no safe way to combine two people's edits (nothing links the two copies back to a shared starting point, so there's nothing to merge against), and no way to find the exact moment a bug was introduced (there's no ordered, inspectable history to search or bisect through). Git's parent-pointer chain solves all three at once, because every commit is explicitly linked to what it came from.

items.prompt: A team wants to know exactly which day a bug was introduced, across dozens of `project-vN.zip` files going back three months. What's the fundamental obstacle, even with unlimited time to look?
choices: There's no ordered, linked history to search through — each zip is an isolated snapshot with no recorded connection to the others
Zip files can't be opened after three months
The bug is probably not actually in any of the zips
Modern computers can't read old zip formats
items.explanation: Even with unlimited patience, a pile of independently-named zips has no structure that supports a targeted search — you'd have to manually diff every pair in some guessed order. Git's commit chain is exactly the ordered, linked structure that makes tools like `git bisect` possible: walk the chain, testing at each point, and converge on the exact commit.

🚫 No mechanism to combine both people's changes

Why: a commit's parent pointer is exactly the missing link — it's what lets Git detect two branches diverged from a common point and merge them.

items.prompt: Besides the actual file contents, what else does a Git commit always record?
choices: Nothing else — a commit is just the file contents, like a zip file
Who made it, when, why (the message), and a pointer to the previous commit
Only the message — timestamps and authorship are optional add-ons
The IP address of the machine that made the commit
items.explanation: A commit is an immutable snapshot plus metadata: author, timestamp, message, and a pointer to its parent commit. That parent pointer is what turns a pile of isolated snapshots into a navigable, ordered chain — the entire history of the project.
items.reference:
👤 Who — author
🕒 When — timestamp
💬 Why — the message
🔗 Parent pointer — link to the previous commit

Why: the parent pointer is the piece a zip filename can never provide — it's what makes history a chain instead of a pile.
items.learnMore:
A commit is snapshot + metadata + link

A zip file has a filename and a modification timestamp from the filesystem — that's it. A commit bundles the actual snapshot with a commit message (the why, written by the person who made the change, at the moment they made it), authorship, and — critically — a pointer to exactly one (or, for a merge, two) parent commits. That pointer is what makes "walk backward through history" a well-defined operation instead of a guess about save order.

items.prompt: Two commits have byte-for-byte identical file contents but different commit messages and timestamps. Are they the same commit?
choices: Yes — content is all that matters for identifying a commit
No — a commit's identity includes its metadata and parent pointer, not just the file contents it snapshots
Only if they're on the same branch
Git would refuse to create the second one as a duplicate
items.explanation: A commit's hash is computed over the snapshot plus its metadata (message, author, timestamp, parent). Two commits can point at identical file contents yet still be different commits, with different hashes, because the message/timestamp/parent differ — content-addressing applies to the underlying file blobs, not to "sameness" of a commit as a whole.
items.reference:
👤 Who — author
🕒 When — timestamp
💬 Why — the message
🔗 Parent pointer — link to the previous commit

Why: the parent pointer is the piece a zip filename can never provide — it's what makes history a chain instead of a pile.

items.prompt: You clone a Git repository and then disconnect from the internet entirely. Which of these can you still do?
choices: Nothing — Git needs a live connection to the remote for every operation
Commit, branch, and view the entire project history, because your clone has the full history, not just the latest snapshot
Only view files, not commit history
Only the most recent 50 commits are available offline
items.explanation: Distributed means every clone has the entire history, not just a pointer to a central server's copy. Committing, branching, and browsing history are all purely local operations against your own copy of the object store — no network round-trip required.
items.reference:
💾 Every clone: the full history, not just the latest snapshot
🌐 No single point of failure
✈️ Commit, branch, browse history — all fully offline

Why: a Git clone isn't a pointer to a remote database — it's a complete, independent copy of the object store.
items.learnMore:
Distributed vs. centralized

Older version-control systems (and manual-copy workflows relying on one shared network drive) had a single authoritative copy — lose it, and you lose the history along with it. Git's clone operation copies the entire object store, not just the current files, which is exactly why push/pull exist as explicit, occasional synchronization steps rather than every command needing the network.

items.prompt: A company's central Git server has a catastrophic hard-drive failure with no backup. What's true about any developer who has a full clone?
choices: They've lost all history too, since the server was authoritative
Their local clone still has the entire project history, and can be used to restore the server
They still have their files, but all commit history is gone for everyone
Only the most recent commit each developer made is recoverable
items.explanation: Because every clone holds the complete history (not a partial cache), any single developer's machine is a full backup of the project's history by construction — this is the practical payoff of "distributed" beyond just working offline.
items.reference:

✈️ Commit, branch, browse history — all fully offline

Why: a Git clone isn't a pointer to a remote database — it's a complete, independent copy of the object store.

items.prompt: Why does every commit pointing to its parent matter, beyond just knowing "what came before"?
choices: It doesn't matter much — the parent pointer is mostly cosmetic
It's what makes "undo to any past state," not just "undo the last action," possible — you can walk the chain back as far as needed
It's only used to display commit messages in order
It exists purely to calculate commit timestamps
items.explanation: Because every commit points to its parent, history forms a walkable chain (a graph once branching is involved). That's what lets you jump back to any past point directly, not just step backward one action at a time the way a simple undo stack would.
items.reference:
A → B → C → D (HEAD)
🎯 Jump straight to A, not just "undo D, then C, then B"

Why: a chain of parent pointers turns "go back to Tuesday" into a direct lookup, not a step-by-step rewind.
items.learnMore:
Why a chain, not a stack

A simple "undo" feature (like Ctrl+Z) only reverses the single most recent action, one at a time, and loses the ability to undo once you've closed the document. Git's commit chain is addressable at every point — git checkout <any past commit hash> jumps directly there, and the chain (or graph, once branches merge) is permanent, not cleared when you close your editor or restart your machine.

items.prompt: Once branching enters the picture, is Git's history still a single straight chain?
choices: Yes, always a single line — branches are just labels on the same chain
No — it becomes a graph, since a commit can have more than one child (branches diverging) or more than one parent (a merge)
No — branching replaces the chain entirely with an unordered set of commits
Yes, because Git forbids more than one branch from existing at a time
items.explanation: A single commit can have multiple children once two branches diverge from it, and a merge commit has two parents — so the overall structure is a directed graph, not a strict line. Each individual commit still points to its parent(s), preserving the same walkable-history property this pool covers.
items.reference:
A → B → C → D (HEAD)
🎯 Jump straight to A, not just "undo D, then C, then B"

Why: a chain of parent pointers turns "go back to Tuesday" into a direct lookup, not a step-by-step rewind.

items.prompt: Why is creating a new Git branch nearly instant, regardless of how large the project is?
choices: Git only creates branches for small projects
A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit — no files are copied or snapshotted to create one
Branch creation happens lazily and doesn't actually finish until the first commit on it
Git compresses the whole project before branching, which is fast on modern hardware
items.explanation: A branch is a small text file holding a commit hash (a pointer), nothing more. Creating one writes that pointer and nothing else — it's O(1) with respect to project size because it never touches the working files or the history that already exists.
items.reference:
🏷️ A branch = a pointer to one commit
⚡ Creating one: write one pointer, done
🚫 No files copied, no snapshot taken

Why: O(1) cost regardless of project size, because branch creation never touches the working files.
items.learnMore:
Branches are cheap by design

Compare this to the manual-copies equivalent of "try an experimental change without risking the working version" — copying the entire project directory, which costs time and disk proportional to project size, every single time. A Git branch is a 40-character commit hash written to a small file under .git/refs/heads/. Nothing about the project's actual files changes until you start committing on the new branch.

items.prompt: In the manual-copies world (no version control), what's the closest equivalent to "try a risky change without touching the working version," and why is it worse than a Git branch?
choices: Editing the file directly and hoping you remember the original — worse because there's no safety net at all
Copying the entire project directory — worse because it's O(project size) in both time and disk, unlike a branch's O(1) pointer
Emailing a copy to a teammate — worse because it introduces a dependency on someone else
There is no equivalent; manual-copy workflows never attempt this
items.explanation: Manual full-directory copies scale with total project size every single time, and multiply the more experimental branches you want to keep around simultaneously — the exact cost a Git branch's pointer-only design avoids entirely.
items.reference:

⚡ Creating one: write one pointer, done
🚫 No files copied, no snapshot taken

Why: O(1) cost regardless of project size, because branch creation never touches the working files.

items.prompt: A developer wants to keep five separate experimental copies of a 2 GB project directory around at once, using manual copies. What's the realistic disk cost, compared to five Git branches on the same project?
choices: About the same either way — disk cost doesn't depend on the mechanism used
Roughly 10 GB for the manual copies (5 × 2 GB), versus roughly 2 GB total for five Git branches, since branches only add pointers, not new file copies
Manual copies would actually use less disk, since zip compression shrinks the files
Git branches would cost more, since Git keeps every branch's full history separately
items.explanation: Five full manual copies of a 2 GB project cost roughly 5×2 GB regardless of how similar they are to each other. Five Git branches on the same repository share the same underlying object store — creating each branch adds a pointer, not a duplicate of the project, so total disk cost stays close to the original 2 GB (plus whatever new commits each branch actually adds).

⚡ Creating one: write one pointer, done
🚫 No files copied, no snapshot taken

Why: O(1) cost regardless of project size, because branch creation never touches the working files.

items.prompt: Two different commits both contain a file with byte-for-byte identical content. How many times does Git actually store that content?
choices: Twice — once per commit, since commits are independent snapshots
Once — Git addresses objects by the hash of their content, so identical content is stored a single time and referenced from both commits
Zero times — Git only stores diffs, and there's no diff between identical files
It depends on whether the two commits are on the same branch
items.explanation: Git's objects are content-addressed: the storage key is a hash of the bytes themselves, not the filename, path, or commit. Identical content anywhere in history hashes to the same key and is physically stored exactly once, referenced by as many commits/trees as need it.
items.reference:
🔑 Storage key = hash of the content itself
🚫 Not the filename, not the path, not the commit
♻️ Identical bytes anywhere → stored once, referenced everywhere

Why: hashing the content itself is what makes deduplication automatic and filename-independent.
items.learnMore:
Content-addressed storage

Every object Git stores (a file's content, a directory listing, a commit) is identified by the SHA-1 hash of its own content. Two files with identical content — even in different commits, branches, or parts of the tree — hash to the same value and are stored exactly once. This is also what makes a commit hash a trustworthy fingerprint of an entire project state: if even one byte anywhere in the tree changed, the commit's hash is different, guaranteed.

items.prompt: A project has two files, `header-old.js` and `header-copy.js`, with completely identical content but different names, sitting in the same commit. Does Git store the content twice?
choices: Yes — different filenames always mean separate storage
No — the storage key is derived from content, not filename, so identical bytes are stored once regardless of how many filenames point to them
Only if they're in different directories
Git would refuse to commit two files with identical content
items.explanation: Filenames live in the tree object (the directory listing), not in the blob (the file content) itself. Two filenames can point at the same content blob, and Git only stores that blob's bytes once — the filenames are just separate references to the same underlying object.
items.reference:
🔑 Storage key = hash of the content itself
🚫 Not the filename, not the path, not the commit
♻️ Identical bytes anywhere → stored once, referenced everywhere

Why: hashing the content itself is what makes deduplication automatic and filename-independent.

items.prompt: You change a single character in a 10,000-line file and commit. What happens to the file's storage key (its content hash)?
choices: It stays the same, since only a tiny fraction of the content changed
It changes completely — even a one-byte difference produces a different hash, unrelated to how small the edit was
It changes only in the last few characters of the hash
Git keeps the old hash and adds a small patch on top
items.explanation: Content hashing has no concept of "mostly the same" — a single changed byte anywhere in the input produces a completely different hash output. That's precisely why an unchanged file across commits keeps the exact same hash (and is deduplicated), while any edit, however tiny, is treated as entirely new content requiring its own storage entry.

items.prompt: You've edited five files, but only three of them belong to the bug fix you're about to describe in a commit message. What does the staging area let you do that a manual-copy save can't?
choices: Nothing different — you'd still have to save everything at once
Stage and commit just the three related files, leaving the other two for a separate, later commit
Delete the other two files automatically
Rename the other two files so they're excluded from future commits permanently
items.explanation: The staging area lets you build a commit out of some of your current changes, not all-or-nothing. Stage the three files that belong to this fix, commit with a message describing exactly that fix, then stage and commit the other two separately — each commit stays a coherent, describable unit.
items.reference:
✅ Stage only what belongs to this commit
📝 Commit with a message describing exactly that
🔁 Repeat for the remaining changes, separately

Why: manual-copy saves are all-or-nothing; staging is what lets a commit stay a coherent, single-purpose unit.
items.learnMore:
Staging as selective commit-building

A manual save (or a naive "save everything" commit) forces every current edit into one lump, whether or not those edits are conceptually related. The staging area is a real, distinct middle state between "edited on disk" and "permanently in history" — it exists specifically so a commit can represent one coherent idea, which is what makes git log readable and git bisect useful later: each commit answers a single "what changed and why."

items.prompt: What's the practical downside of a version-control model that skipped staging and went straight from "edited on disk" to "committed," with no in-between step?
choices: There's no real downside — staging is just extra ceremony
Every commit would necessarily include every current edit, making it hard to keep commits focused on one coherent change
Commits would become smaller and more frequent automatically
It would make branching impossible
items.explanation: Without a staging step, "commit" would have to mean "commit everything currently changed," forcing unrelated edits into the same snapshot. Staging is what decouples "what's changed on disk" from "what goes into the next commit," letting each commit stay focused.
items.reference:
✅ Stage only what belongs to this commit
📝 Commit with a message describing exactly that
🔁 Repeat for the remaining changes, separately

Why: manual-copy saves are all-or-nothing; staging is what lets a commit stay a coherent, single-purpose unit.

items.prompt: Why does Git compute diffs on demand for display, rather than storing them?
choices: Because storing diffs is technically impossible
Because what's stored is complete snapshots, and a diff between two snapshots can always be recomputed later — storing it separately would be redundant
Because diffs are only useful for text files, not binaries
Because Git actually does store diffs, just compressed
items.explanation: Since each commit is a full, independently addressable snapshot, the difference between any two commits is fully determined by comparing those two snapshots — there's nothing extra to precompute or store. Computing it on demand keeps storage simple (snapshots only) at the cost of a cheap computation at display time.
items.reference:
💾 Stored: full snapshots, deduplicated by content
🖥️ Computed on demand: the diff shown by git diff

Why: a diff between two full snapshots is always recomputable, so storing it separately would just be redundant.
items.learnMore:
Snapshots as the single source of truth

Because a diff is a pure function of two snapshots (old and new), storing both the snapshots and the diff would be duplicating derivable information. Git keeps the storage model simple — snapshots, content-addressed — and lets any display or comparison tool (git diff, git log -p, a GUI) recompute the diff whenever it's actually needed.

items.prompt: If Git only stores full snapshots and computes diffs on demand, what determines how expensive `git diff` between two arbitrary commits is?
choices: How many commits apart they are in history
The size of the two snapshots being compared, since the diff is computed fresh from them each time, independent of how many commits separate them
It's always instant regardless of size, since diffs are cached permanently
It depends on which branch each commit is on
items.explanation: Since a diff is computed directly from the two full snapshots being compared, its cost depends on the size/complexity of those two snapshots — not on how many commits sit between them in history. Comparing commit #1 and commit #1000 is no more expensive than comparing two adjacent commits of similar size.
items.reference:
💾 Stored: full snapshots, deduplicated by content
🖥️ Computed on demand: the diff shown by git diff

Why: a diff between two full snapshots is always recomputable, so storing it separately would just be redundant.

Because a diff is a pure function of two snapshots (old and new), storing both the snapshots and the diff would be duplicating derivable information. Git keeps the storage model simple — snapshots, content-addressed — and lets any display or comparison tool (git diff, git log -p, a GUI) recompute the diff whenever it's actually needed.

items.prompt: Why does content-addressing make a commit hash a trustworthy "fingerprint" of an entire project state?
choices: Because the hash is randomly generated and unrelated to content
Because if even one byte anywhere in the tree changed, the resulting hash is guaranteed to be different
Because Git manually verifies each commit against a checksum server
Because commit hashes are assigned sequentially, like version numbers
items.explanation: Since every object (blob, tree, commit) is hashed from its own content, and a tree's hash depends on the hashes of everything inside it, a single changed byte anywhere ripples upward and changes the commit's hash too. Two different commit hashes are therefore a reliable signal that something, somewhere in the tree, differs.
items.reference:
🌳 A tree's hash depends on every object's hash inside it
💥 One changed byte, anywhere → the commit hash changes too

Why: hashes compose upward, so a commit hash is effectively a fingerprint of the entire tree beneath it.
items.learnMore:
Hashes compose upward

A commit object references a tree object (the root directory listing), which references blob objects (file contents) and further tree objects (subdirectories), each identified by its own content hash. Changing a single file changes that blob's hash, which changes the tree that references it, which changes the commit that references that tree — the change propagates all the way up, which is exactly why two identical commit hashes are a reliable guarantee of byte-for-byte identical project state.

Always — hashes only depend on file contents, and both did the same edits
Only if they're using the exact same operating system

items.prompt: A very old commit and the current HEAD are 900 commits apart. What does Git actually do when you run `git diff <old-commit> HEAD`?
choices: It replays and combines the diffs of all 900 intermediate commits in order
It compares the two full snapshots directly, ignoring everything in between
It refuses, since diffs across more than 100 commits aren't supported
It only shows the diff of the most recent 10 commits by default
items.explanation: Since every commit is a full, independently addressable snapshot, comparing any two of them (however far apart in history) is a direct comparison of those two snapshots — Git never needs to replay or accumulate the commits in between.
items.reference:
💾 Stored: full snapshots, deduplicated by content
🖥️ Computed on demand: the diff shown by git diff

Why: a diff between two full snapshots is always recomputable directly, regardless of how many commits sit between them.
items.learnMore:
Diffs are always two-snapshot comparisons

Because history is a chain (or graph) of independently addressable full snapshots, git diff A B is defined purely in terms of A and B — it doesn't matter how many commits happen to sit between them chronologically. This is a direct consequence of storing snapshots instead of incremental diffs, and it's part of why operations like checking out a commit from years ago cost the same as checking out yesterday's.

items.prompt: Content-addressed storage means identical content is only ever stored once, no matter how many places reference it. Implement `dedupeByContent(files)`, which takes an array of file content strings and returns an array of the *unique* content strings, in the order each first appeared — modeling the core idea behind Git's object store.

tests.description: removes exact duplicates
preserves first-occurrence order
returns everything when all unique
handles an empty list

items.explanation: A `Set` keyed on the content itself (a stand-in for Git's content hash) is exactly the deduplication mechanism content-addressed storage relies on: checking 'have I already stored this exact content?' before storing it again, rather than blindly appending every occurrence.
items.reference:
📥 Input: ["a", "b", "a", "c"]
📤 Output: ["a", "b", "c"] — "a" kept once, at its first position

Why: Git's object store checks "do I already have this exact content?" before writing anything new, exactly like a Set lookup.
items.learnMore:
Content-addressed dedup, modeled

Git never asks "is this the same file as before?" — it asks "do I already have an object with this exact content hash?" A `Set` keyed on the content string is a faithful (if simplified — Git uses a real SHA-1 hash, not the raw string) model of that check: seen-before content is skipped, never-seen content is added once. This is the same idea the interactive demo on L2 quantifies with real byte counts.

items.prompt: Model a minimal version of Git's object store. Implement `writeObject(store, content)`, where `store` is a `Map` from key to content. Use `simpleHash(content)` (given below, already implemented) as the key. If the key already exists in `store`, don't overwrite it (it's already there — dedup). Return the key either way.

tests.description: writing new content adds it to the store
tests.expr: const s = new Map(); const k = writeObject(s, 'hello'); expect(s.get(k)).toBe('hello')

tests.description: writing identical content twice keeps the store at size 1
tests.expr: const s = new Map(); writeObject(s, 'hello'); writeObject(s, 'hello'); expect(s.size).toBe(1)

tests.description: identical content always returns the same key
tests.expr: const s = new Map(); const k1 = writeObject(s, 'x'); const k2 = writeObject(s, 'x'); expect(k1).toBe(k2)

tests.description: different content produces different keys and grows the store
tests.expr: const s = new Map(); writeObject(s, 'a'); writeObject(s, 'b'); expect(s.size).toBe(2)

items.explanation: This is content-addressed storage in miniature: the key is derived purely from the content (via `simpleHash`, standing in for Git's real SHA-1), never from a filename or call order. Checking `store.has(key)` before writing is exactly the dedup step — identical content always hashes to the same key, so a second write of the same content is a no-op that still correctly returns the existing key.
items.reference:
🔑 key = simpleHash(content)
❓ store.has(key)? skip write : store.set(key, content)
↩️ Always return key, written or not

Why: this is exactly what git hash-object -w does — compute the key, write only if it's genuinely new.
items.learnMore:

Git's real object store works the same way, with a cryptographic hash instead of `simpleHash`: compute a key purely from content, check whether that key already exists in .git/objects/, and only write new bytes to disk if it doesn't. `writeObject` above is a faithful, runnable miniature of that mechanism — the L3 section's `hash-object.mjs` example shows the real SHA-1 version producing output that matches git hash-object exactly.

items.prompt: Implement `gitStorageKB(numCommits, projectSizeKB, changedFraction)`: the first commit stores the full project once; every commit after that only adds `projectSizeKB * changedFraction` (the changed slice — the rest is already deduplicated). Return 0 if `numCommits` is 0 or less.

tests.description: zero commits means zero storage
one commit costs exactly the full project size
later commits only add the changed fraction each time
a 0% changed fraction means storage never grows past the first commit

items.explanation: This is the exact formula behind the L2 interactive demo and the L3 `storage-estimate.mjs` example: one full copy up front (nothing exists yet to deduplicate against), then only the changed slice per commit afterward, because the unchanged remainder is already in the object store and gets referenced again for free.
items.reference:
1️⃣ First commit: full project size, once
➕ Every commit after: only the changed slice

Why: the unchanged remainder of the project is already stored from a previous commit, so it's referenced again, not re-copied.
items.learnMore:
Modeling storage growth

Compare this to `manualCopyStorageKB(numCommits, projectSizeKB) = numCommits * projectSizeKB` — every manual save is a completely independent full copy, so its cost is strictly linear in the number of saves. Git's cost is linear too, but in the changed amount rather than the total project size, which is why the gap between the two widens the more commits accumulate, exactly as the L2 interactive demo shows when you drag numCommits up.

items.prompt: Given an array of file status objects like `{ name: 'a.js', status: 'staged' | 'modified' | 'committed' }`, implement `nextCommitFiles(files)` returning the names of only the files that would actually be included if `git commit` ran right now — i.e. only the `'staged'` ones.

tests.description: includes only staged files
excludes already-committed files with no new staged change
returns multiple staged files in order
returns an empty array when nothing is staged

items.explanation: Only files in the 'staged' state are included in the next commit — 'modified' means edited on disk but never `git add`-ed, and 'committed' means already in history with no new staged change since. This filter is the direct model of what `git commit` actually reads from: the staging area, not the whole working directory.
items.reference:
💻 modified — edited, never staged
📥 staged — will be in the next commit
🗄️ committed — already in history

Why: git commit only ever reads from the staging area — a 'modified' file with no staged change is silently left out.
items.learnMore:
What a commit actually reads

This is the exact mistake the L3 failure-modes section warns about: forgetting to git add a file before committing means it's edited and visible on disk, but its status is still 'modified,' not 'staged' — so git commit silently leaves it out, with no error. Checking git status before every commit is the habit that catches this, because it explicitly separates staged changes from unstaged ones in its output.

items.prompt: You edit `utils.js`, then run `git commit -m "Fix date formatting"` without running `git add` first. What happens?
choices: Git commits automatically includes every changed file, staged or not
The commit succeeds, but `utils.js`'s changes are silently excluded, since only staged changes are committed
Git refuses to commit until every changed file is staged
Git stages the file automatically the first time you commit
items.explanation: `git commit` only writes the staging area's contents into history. An edited-but-never-staged file simply isn't part of the next commit — no error, no warning by default, just a commit that quietly doesn't include the change you meant to make.
items.reference:
✏️ Edited utils.js
🚫 Never ran git add
🤫 Commit succeeds — silently missing the change

Why: git commit reads only from staging — a modified-but-unstaged file is invisible to it.
items.learnMore:
The forgotten-add trap

This is a very common beginner trap precisely because the commit doesn't fail — it succeeds, with a plausible-looking message, just missing the file you meant to include. `git status` immediately before every commit is the specific habit that prevents this: it always shows exactly what's staged (will be committed) vs. what's merely modified (won't be), catching the mistake before it becomes a confusing "why didn't my fix work" investigation later.

items.prompt: A team commits a 50 MB video file 20 times, changing a few frames each time. Why does the repository's size grow roughly linearly with every version, unlike a text file with the same edit pattern?
choices: Video files are always excluded from Git's object store automatically
There's no meaningful line-based diff for a binary, so content-addressing stores a new full copy of the blob every time even one byte changes
Git compresses binaries so effectively that repeated commits cost almost nothing
Binary files can only be committed once per repository
items.explanation: Content-addressing dedupes identical content, but a changed binary is entirely new content from Git's point of view — there's no sub-file diffing the way there is for text, so even a tiny visual change to one frame produces a completely different blob hash, and the full new blob gets stored.
items.reference:
📄 Text file, small edit: new blob is mostly redundant with old, but still a full new blob
🎞️ Binary file, small edit: a completely different blob, full size, every time

Why: content-addressing dedupes identical content, not similar content — a changed binary is entirely new content, full stop.
items.learnMore:
Why binaries defeat content-addressing's efficiency

Content-addressing stores a new full copy of a binary blob every time even one byte changes, so repeatedly committing changing binaries grows the repository's size roughly linearly with every version ever committed — close to the manual-copies growth curve this entire unit contrasts Git against, not the deduplicated one. This is the practical reason large media/data usually lives outside Git proper (object storage, Git LFS) rather than committed directly: the storage-savings argument this unit makes for text and source code simply doesn't apply the same way.

items.prompt: Why doesn't Git's content-addressing help much when a large binary file changes slightly, the way it helps for a text file's small edit?
choices: It helps exactly the same amount for both — file type doesn't matter to content-addressing
Content-addressing only dedupes byte-identical content; a changed binary produces entirely different bytes end-to-end, with no partial reuse of the old version's storage
Git specifically detects binary files and refuses to deduplicate them on purpose
Binary files are stored uncompressed, which is unrelated to deduplication
items.explanation: Deduplication only saves storage for bytes that are exactly identical to something already stored. A small visual/audio edit to a binary file typically changes the encoded byte stream throughout (not just a small contiguous region the way a text edit does), so the new blob shares little or nothing with the old one at the byte level — full storage cost, every time.

items.prompt: A project's `node_modules/` folder (hundreds of MB, fully regeneratable from `package.json`) gets committed by accident. What does content-addressing do about this on its own?
choices: Nothing — Git happily stores and diffs all of it forever unless a `.gitignore` deliberately excludes it
Git automatically detects and excludes dependency folders by name
Content-addressing deduplicates it down to almost nothing, since dependency files rarely change
Git refuses to commit folders larger than 50 MB
items.explanation: Git has no built-in notion of "this doesn't belong" — content-addressing happily stores and diffs whatever you point it at, generated noise included. A `.gitignore` is a deliberate, human-authored exclusion list; without one, every regeneratable file gets committed and permanently bloats the repository's history.
items.reference:
📦 node_modules/ — hundreds of MB, fully regeneratable
🤷 Git has no opinion — it'll store and diff it forever
📝 .gitignore — the deliberate fix

Why: content-addressing is a storage mechanism, not a judgment about what's worth storing — that judgment has to be authored explicitly.
items.learnMore:
Content-addressing doesn't imply curation

It's tempting to assume "Git is smart about storage" extends to "Git is smart about what belongs in history" — it isn't. Content-addressing solves the narrower, mechanical problem of not re-storing identical bytes; it says nothing about whether those bytes should have been committed in the first place. Dependency folders, build output, and `.env` files with real secrets all need a deliberately maintained `.gitignore`, because Git will store and permanently retain anything it's asked to, generated noise included.

items.prompt: Once a large `node_modules/` folder has been committed and later added to `.gitignore`, does the repository immediately shrink back down?
choices: Yes — `.gitignore` retroactively removes anything matching it from history
No — `.gitignore` only prevents *future* commits from including it; the already-committed copies remain in history until deliberately rewritten out
Yes, but only after running `git gc`
No — the folder has to be deleted from disk for `.gitignore` to take effect at all
items.explanation: `.gitignore` is forward-looking: it tells Git which untracked files to stop offering up for staging going forward. Content that's already committed is already part of permanent history — content-addressing means it's still sitting in the object store, referenced by every commit that included it, and removing it requires deliberately rewriting history (a separate, more invasive operation), not just adding a `.gitignore` entry.
